title: CMS, content models and languages
summary: Keep content consistent, reusable and safe to publish.
why: Structured content reduces duplicate entry and supports automated validation.
Sources, versions and owners keep migrated content maintainable.
know: Define content types such as articles, services and products before fields, relationships and validation.
Decide markets, URLs, fallbacks and translation status. Share facts; adapt copy to each market.
Assign responsibility for preview, review, publication and media rights. API access is separate from what the page displays.
inputs: Content and URL inventory, fields and assets
Markets, languages, editing workflow, existing CMS and integrations
actions: Create schemas, sample records, source mappings and required-field validation.
Use repeatable transformations for content, media and relationships; start with a dry run.
Check counts, content, URLs, previews and permissions. Document the editing process.
done: Important records map from old to new, with a list of missing items.
Public APIs and search cannot expose unpublished material.
pitfalls: Using a page-sized HTML blob as the only content model.
Checking record counts without checking images and relationships.
decision: Agree on content owners, publishing permissions and changes that need review.

reader.concept: A CMS stores and manages website content. A content model defines fields for articles, products and cases so the same data can be reused.
reader.when: Use this when updates are slow, pages disagree or the site needs more languages.

example.situation: A product name is typed separately on the homepage, comparison table and blog.
example.lesson: Store shared facts once so updates stay consistent.

reader.first_step: Pick frequently updated content and list its fields, sources and uses.
terms: A content management system for editing and publishing.
The version used when the requested content is missing.
